strengths: First systematic exploration of SSM (Mamba-2) backbones for masked discrete diffusion language models, filling a clear gap between vision-domain Mamba-diffusion work and text DLMs that remain Transformer-bound.

Controlled, apples-to-apples comparison across three model scales (240M, 0.5B, 1.3B) with matched training data, tokenization, noise schedule, decoding steps, and approximate compute budgets (Chinchilla and Quokka), isolating the effect of backbone architecture.

Thorough throughput/latency analysis across a wide range of sequence lengths (32 to 65K), supported by a plausible theoretical complexity argument (linear vs. quadratic scaling) that matches the empirical curves in Figure 2, giving good insight into why and when the gains occur.

The hybrid DiffuApriel-H design is a sensible and well-motivated middle ground, and the paper shows it is competitive or best in perplexity/downstream accuracy while still providing substantial speedups, illustrating a useful attention-recurrence trade-off for diffusion denoisers.

Reasonably broad evaluation suite (validation PPL, 7 zero-shot PPL benchmarks, and downstream accuracy on 5-6 reasoning/commonsense tasks) showing consistent (if modest) gains for Mamba/hybrid variants over the Transformer DLM baseline.
weaknesses: Throughput/latency measurements are reported only at batch size 1; no batched-inference or serving-realistic throughput numbers are given, which is a significant gap since real deployment typically uses batching and KV-cache reuse patterns that could change relative advantages.

No actual generation-quality evaluation (e.g., generative perplexity via an external scorer, sample quality, or human/LLM-judged coherence) is reported — the paper relies entirely on likelihood-based metrics (validation/zero-shot PPL) and standard zero-shot accuracy, leaving open whether the Mamba/hybrid denoiser produces qualitatively comparable generations at various denoising step budgets.

The number of denoising steps is fixed at S=128 throughout; there is no exploration of the quality-speed trade-off as steps are reduced, which is central to whether the throughput gains translate into practical end-to-end speedups for actual multi-step decoding (not just raw per-step FLOPs/latency scaling).
The hybrid interleaving hyperparameter K=5 is fixed without ablation or justification; no sensitivity analysis of how varying K affects the throughput/quality trade-off is provided.

Perplexity results are somewhat inconsistent — at the smallest scale (240M) DiffuApriel is frequently worse than DiffuTran (e.g., PTB, WikiText, LM1B), and the paper's narrative of a monotonic trend with scale is not fully supported by Table 3 nor discussed critically.

The bidirectional Mamba fusion uses simple additive combination of forward/backward hidden states (Eq. 6) without ablating this design choice against other fusion strategies (e.g., concatenation, gating), leaving the architectural decision underexplored.

Limitations discussion is very brief (a single sentence about short-context regimes); other important limitations (e.g., lack of larger-scale validation beyond 1.3B, no long-context task evaluation such as retrieval/needle-in-haystack despite motivating long-context efficiency, absence of code/checkpoint release) are not addressed.

No direct comparison against existing Transformer-based DLM acceleration techniques (approximate KV-caching methods cited in related work) is provided, even though these are the most relevant practical baselines for throughput improvement; they are dismissed as 'orthogonal' without empirical contextualization.
Redundant/overlapping appendix Table 5 duplicates Table 4 with an added MMLU column and slightly different numbers, which is confusing and suggests some lack of care in final compilation of results.

strengths: Genuine and timely architectural contribution: to the authors' knowledge, this is the first work combining state-space (Mamba-2) backbones with masked discrete diffusion language modeling, filling a clear gap between the vision-diffusion-Mamba literature and text DLMs.

Well-controlled experimental design: DiffuTran, DiffuApriel, and DiffuApriel-H are trained with identical data (DCLM), tokenizer, noise schedule, decoding steps, and compute budgets across three scales (240M/0.5B/1.3B), isolating the effect of the mixer architecture.

The efficiency analysis is grounded in a clear theoretical cost model (O(BLd) vs O(BL^2d) vs the hybrid interpolation) that is directly validated by the empirical throughput/latency curves in Figure 2, giving the efficiency claims good internal consistency.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: validation perplexity under two compute-optimal budgets, zero-shot perplexity on 7 held-out corpora, and downstream zero-shot accuracy on 5-6 commonsense/reasoning benchmarks, with trends that are largely consistent (hybrid variant improving with scale).

The hybrid design (interleaving attention every K layers) is a sensible and practically motivated architecture that retains some global context modeling while preserving most of the efficiency benefit, and the paper is transparent that this idea is inspired by existing AR hybrid literature rather than claimed as fully novel.
weaknesses: No comparison against actual published SOTA diffusion LMs (e.g., LLaDA, Dream-7B, MDLM) — DiffuTran is an internally trained baseline, so it is unclear whether the reported gains would hold or shrink against stronger/better-tuned Transformer DLM baselines, or whether DiffuTran itself is a representative/well-tuned baseline.

No generation-quality evaluation beyond likelihood-based metrics (perplexity, downstream accuracy); no sample-based metrics (e.g., MAUVE, human/LLM-judged quality, generative PPL under a proxy model) are reported, which is important since diffusion LMs' practical value is in generation quality, not just held-out likelihood.

Model scale is modest (up to 1.3B params, 120B tokens) and downstream accuracies remain near chance-level for several tasks (Table 4/5), making it hard to confidently extrapolate whether Mamba/hybrid advantages persist at scales where diffusion LMs are actually competitive with strong AR models (7B+).

Throughput/latency comparisons are only reported at batch size 1 (Section 4.1), which does not reflect realistic serving conditions where batching interacts differently with quadratic attention vs. linear SSM costs; no results at batch>1 or with actual serving-style continuous batching are given.

Design choices such as additive fusion of forward/backward Mamba streams (Eq. 6) and fixed interleaving frequency K=5 for the hybrid model are not ablated, so it is unclear how sensitive results are to these architectural hyperparameters.

Mixed/inconsistent zero-shot results at the smallest scale (Table 3, e.g., PTB perplexity of DiffuApriel is substantially worse than DiffuTran at 240M) are not thoroughly discussed or explained, weakening the narrative that Mamba backbones are uniformly competitive at all scales.

Minor inconsistency between abstract (4.4x) and body/figure captions (5.3x for DiffuApriel, 4.4x for DiffuApriel+MLP) regarding the headline throughput number, which could mislead readers skimming only the abstract.

Reproducibility details (optimizer, learning rate schedule, exact training compute/FLOPs, code/checkpoint release) are not clearly specified in the main text, limiting independent verification of the reported numbers.

strengths: Novel and timely combination: this appears to be the first systematic study of replacing Transformer denoisers with (bidirectional) Mamba-2 mixers in masked discrete diffusion LMs for text, an underexplored intersection given SSMs' success in AR LMs and Mamba's use in vision diffusion.

Controlled, architecture-isolated comparison: DiffuTran, DiffuMamba, and DiffuMamba-H are trained under identical data, tokenization, noise schedule, and roughly matched parameter budgets across three scales (240M, 0.5B, 1.3B), which strengthens the causal attribution of observed differences to the backbone choice.

Thorough efficiency analysis combining asymptotic complexity (Table 3) with empirical throughput/latency measurements across a wide range of sequence lengths (64 to 260K tokens) and multiple decoding strategies (full-sequence, Fast-dLLM block-cache, block-autoregressive caching), which is a valuable systematic contribution beyond just proposing a new model.

The latency-decomposition experiment (fitting quadratic/linear/constant components) provides a clean, interpretable explanation for why Mamba-based denoisers scale better, adding mechanistic insight rather than just headline throughput numbers.

Reasonably transparent reporting: detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix, an explicit limitations section, and acknowledgment that the best-performing inference configuration (Mamba + block cache) has not yet been trained end-to-end for that regime.
weaknesses: Benefits of the Mamba backbone are inconsistent at smaller scale: at 240M parameters, DiffuTran actually wins on 4/7 zero-shot datasets and has better validation PPL under some budgets, undermining the generality of the central claim and suggesting the advantage may be scale-dependent or partly an artifact of the specific MLP-ratio rebalancing used to match parameter counts.

Downstream zero-shot accuracies (Table 4) are very close to random-guess baselines for multiple-choice tasks (e.g., ARC ~25-28%, OBQA ~26-34%), so the claimed ~4% average improvement, while numerically present, provides weak evidence of meaningfully better reasoning/knowledge capability at this scale; error bars/seeds are not reported to assess significance.

The strongest efficiency configuration (DiffuMamba + block-cache) is only evaluated using a training-free/off-the-shelf caching adaptation rather than a model actually trained with block-diffusion inductive biases, which the authors themselves note is left to future work — this means the paper's most compelling throughput number is not paired with an equally validated quality guarantee.

Throughput comparisons depend on a chosen denoising-step scaling law (K = L/p for p in {8,16}); it is unclear whether these step counts yield comparable generation quality across DiffuTran vs. DiffuMamba variants at long lengths, so the fairness of the throughput-at-equal-quality comparison is not fully established.

All throughput/latency experiments use batch size 1 only; production serving scenarios typically use larger batches where memory-bandwidth bottlenecks and relative gains from linear-time mixers could differ substantially, and this is only acknowledged as a limitation rather than explored.

No qualitative/human evaluation of generation quality (coherence, diversity, self-correction ability) is provided; the paper relies entirely on perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy, leaving open whether the parallel/self-correcting properties that motivate DLMs are preserved with the Mamba backbone.

Limited comparison to alternative linear/hybrid mixers (e.g., gated linear attention, RWKV-style recurrences) or other SSM variants, so it is unclear whether Mamba-2 specifically is necessary or whether the gains generalize to other linear-time mixers claimed as future work.

Scale remains modest (up to 1.3B) relative to current practical LLM/DLM deployments, and given that hybridization benefits appear to grow with scale, it is uncertain whether conclusions extrapolate to the multi-billion parameter regimes where these efficiency gains would matter most in practice.
